The next review point is watchdog failure. A lease timer only helps if a watchdog crash also stops the product. The workers are settling that process-control boundary before implementing the renewal protocol.

I rejected a restart-only watchdog design because it could leave the product running if the watchdog kept failing. We’re narrowing this toward supervision inside the collector’s existing systemd unit, so a collector failure also terminates its child processes.

The revised design uses the collector as the supervisor and systemd as its backstop: lease loss stops the evaluator, and missing collector heartbeats cause systemd to kill the cgroup. Lease records will include the VM boot identity so a reboot cannot make an old lease valid again.

We found the original Azure deployment, with all three task VMs deallocated. I’ve authorized starting only the validation VM to recover the pinned artifacts and, later, test the controls with a fake child process. The other two VMs will stay off.

The lock-timing fix is in place. Review also caught a process-group issue: the `/usr/bin/time` wrapper can exit before its child does. Shutdown now checks the whole process group before reporting it stopped, and the test worker is exercising that with a small local child process.

Review found a deployment-specific bug before launch: renewal runs as root, but the collector runs as `graphcheck`. Atomic renewal would have made the lease file root-only and stopped the collector on its first renewal. The fix will preserve ownership, and the live smoke will use the real split of users.

The ownership fix is in, and controller state writes are now atomic so an interrupted renewal cannot corrupt the recovery handle. The workers are finishing the combined checks and the real-user systemd smoke test before the single diagnostic is admitted.

The signal-format regression now passes, including rejection of the wrong signal. The corrected smoke is being rerun under `graphcheck` with root renewal. If it passes, we can commit the harness and freeze the final one-request package.

The root launcher will capture that identity before starting the unit, and the collector will compare its own namespace against it.
